provenance.orgName: Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire. Benedictine abbey of St Mary the Virgin and St Modwenna
provenance.p: Provenance is inferred from the contents, the so-called Burton Annals. The manuscript comprises three discrete parts: (1) fols. 4–108 + 117–178; (2) fols. 109–116; (3) fols. 179–203. Whereas NRK in MLGB2 assigned only 'article 1' to Burton, meaning the Annals in fols. 4–108, the near-identical ruling and layout of the miscellany on fols. 117–178 mean that this portion may also be assigned to Burton. In this later section, constitutions of two bishops of Coventry and Lichfield, William of Cornhill and Alexander of Stavensby, give weight to the suggestion. It follows that part 2, an interposed quire, was also from Burton. The provenance of article 3 is unclear and may have been added to the assemblage by either Christ Church or, more likely, Cotton. Ex inf. Ralph Hanna.

history.provenance: Christ Church, Oxford. Traded with Sir Robert Cotton for what is now Christ Church, MS 343, according to a note in the latter.

Sir Robert Bruce Cotton, 1st baronet of Connington (1571–1631), antiquary and politician. (Table of contents written by his librarian, Richard James, on fol. 2r; Cotton's own instructions to his binder, fol. 1r; bookplate).

Cotton’s library passed to his son, Sir Thomas Cotton (1594–1662), 2nd baronet, and his grandson, Sir John Cotton (1621–1702), 3rd baronet. This last bequeathed the Cotton collection of books and manuscripts to trustees 'for Publick Use and Advantage', under terms incorporated in an Act of 1700 (12 and 13 William III, c. 7). It formed one of the foundation collections of the British Museum in 1753.

recordHist.source: Richard Sharpe and James M. W. Willoughby, eds, Medieval Libraries of Great Britain, 2010–15.
